speechtext: Mr. Speaker, following the traditional course I wish to announce the appointment of the under secretary of state and deputy registrar general of Canada in the person of Mr. Jean Miquelon, Q.C., of Danville and Montreal. Mr. Miquelon studied law at Laval University and was admitted to the bar of the province of Quebec in 1934. He joined the Canadian army in 1941, following a period of service as crown prosecutor in Val d'Or. He spent several years overseas and became deputy judge advocate general of the Canadian army occupation force in Germany; returned to Canada with the rank of major and resumed legal practice in Montreal. Mr. Miquelon served as the Quebec representative on the dominion command of the Royal Canadian Legion from 1955 to 1960, and in the latter year was elected vice-chairman of the Legion's dominion command. He is recognized as a distinguished member of the bar, and the government is pleased that a man of his capacity is available to accept this appointment.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DISARMAMENT CONFERENCE-REPORT BV EXTERNAL AFFAIRS MINISTER
speechtext:
No doubt, Mr. Speaker, the house would be interested in having a brief report on the disarmament conference which has now been under way in Geneva for over two weeks.
Canada has been very deeply interested in this disarmament conference. Hon. members know our nation was a member of the 10 nation disarmament committee which broke down in June, 1960. A few weeks later Canada and the United States took steps to bring about a meeting of the disarmament commission of the United Nations. That was held, I think, on August 18, 1960, and after some trials and tribulations, a unanimous resolution was put through calling for an immediate resumption of disarmament negotiations.
As we all know, nothing happened, and at the meeting of the general assembly of that fall and at every opportunity at the United Nations since that time Canada has been, I think I can fairly say, taking the lead in demanding that disarmament negotiations be resumed; also that there be added to any disarmament committee representatives of the unaligned nations, and that any such committee should be more closely under the United Nations.
The conference now taking place at Geneva meets all these conditions and for that reason, if for no other-and of course the main reason for our interest is the vital importance of the question of disarmament and of putting an end to the nuclear weapons race-Canada is very pleased that the disarmament conference has been set up in the way in which it has been and with the way the conference is now taking place in Geneva.
One of the main features, of course, is that we now have the two great nuclear powers,

Geneva Disarmament Conference the United States and the Soviet union, negotiating. They are right there, talking to each other, and in addition they are the joint co-chairmen of this conference. That has never been the case before. In the conference on Laos, where the British and Russians were joint co-chairmen, we thought the results of that particular set-up were excellent, and we pressed before the disarmament conference commenced for a similar arrangement at this conference under which the United States and the Soviet union would accept the joint co-chairmanship; because if they do not reach agreement then there is not going to be any agreement reached that is of any value. I think there is great merit in placing the responsibility right on the shoulders of the representatives of these two great nations.
This was agreed to by the other members of the western five. We also placed the suggestion before the Soviet union and the eight non-aligned countries which are participating, and eventually when the conference met agreement was reached that the United States and the Soviet union would accept this responsibility. So there they are, their representatives talking together every day and many times a day; they have to come to terms on procedure and the subjects to be discussed, and I think this is a very sensible arrangement and one which could make all the difference between the success or failure of the conference.
As we all know, there are eight non-aligned countries participating; India and Burma from Asia; Sweden from Europe; the United Arab Republic, Nigeria and Ethiopia from Africa, and Mexico and Brazil from Latin America. These are all countries which have been very much interested in the question of disarmament. Canada's relations with each and every one of them are excellent, and the foreign ministers or heads of delegations of those countries were in Geneva determined to try to bridge the gap between the so-called western and communist nations.
In my judgment these men and women are doing an excellent job. The head of the Swedish delegation now is a woman, Mrs. Myrdal, who is a member of the Swedish senate, and I am awfully glad she is there. I hope she will tell the men to stop arguing and fighting whenever the need for such advice arises. She will be listened to far more than a Canadian man would be, for example, or a man from any other country. I believe these representatives are there in a spirit of dedication to the cause of world peace. The very fact that these eight non-aligned countries are represented is another very hopeful feature of the conference.
So far as the connection with the United Nations is concerned, the conference was set

up by a resolution of the United Nations. There is a representative of the secretary general there in addition to other officials, and the conference has to report to the United Nations disarmament commission by June 1. This is another extremely important factor, because in this situation time is of the essence. The conference could easily drag on and on, as earlier disarmament conferences tended to do, but it is faced with a deadline by which an interim report must be made to the United Nations disarmament commission. So in all these three respects the conference meets Canada's wishes.
Now the first stage is over. The conference has been organized in a reasonable way. The main objective, of course, is to work out an agreement on disarmament, a disarmament treaty. This is to be undertaken by the conference meeting in plenary session. It is regarded as the main job. Yesterday, for example, the conference met in plenary session and was working on a draft preamble to a treaty. I am hopeful that before too long it will be possible to reach agreement on a preamble. The Russians have submitted a draft treaty with a preamble and the United States has a draft disarmament program which also contains a preamble. Canada has some ideas about what should be in the preamble as well, and I hope that before too long it will be possible to get a small drafting group to sit down and actually write out the terms of a preamble for such a treaty. Then the aim is to go on section by section and, where a section is difficult and agreement cannot be reached, to set it aside for the time being and deal with other sections on which it is more likely there can be agreement. This was the method followed at the Laos conference with greatest success.
Then in addition-and I think Canada can take some credit for this-there has been set up a committee of the whole on initial or collateral measures. We very soon decided that there were some issues which, although not directly related to disarmament-they would not necessarily be in a disarmament treaty-were nevertheless capable of an agreed solution with the result that tension could be reduced. The viewpoint was generally held that it was worth while trying to reach agreement on some of these collateral measures, and this committee was designed for that purpose.
We were a little afraid there would be delay in actually getting that committee working, although it had been agreed that there would be such a committee. So on Monday there was a debate in plenary session council and we suggested that this committee should get to work. In order to give its members something to work on and also to start the

wheels turning we recommended that the committee should first consider the question of outer space. We submitted a draft declaration in the following terms:
The governments of Brazil, the People's Republic of Bulgaria, Burma, Canada, the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic, Ethiopia, India, Italy, Mexico, Nigeria, the People's Republic of Poland, the People's Republic of Rumania, Sweden, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, the United Arab Republic, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and the United States of America, desiring to facilitate the achievement of an international agreement to ensure that outer space will be used for peaceful purposes only, solemnly declare that henceforth:
(a)	the orbiting or stationing in outer space of devices for delivering weapons of mass destruction shall be prohibited;
(b)	they will give advance notification of launchings of space vehicles and missiles to the secretary general of the United Nations, and, upon its establishment, to the international disarmament organization.
We believed and still believe that a declaration of that kind would be of great value, and we see no reason why agreement should not be reached on it. I point out that neither side now has weapons of mass destruction in orbit so that a declaration of this type, if adopted, would be before the event. I suggest it is much easier and wiser to have questions of this kind agreed to before there are weapons of mass destruction out in orbit than it would be after such weapons are in orbit. Once they were in outer space it would be a much more difficult task to reach agreement of this kind.
As I have pointed out, we asked that there be a meeting of the committee of the whole on initial collateral measures and that was agreed to. The committee met on Wednesday. Several other countries had suggestions to offer. The communist countries wanted to consider the question of atom free zones, and there were various other suggestions; for example, the question of surprise attack, and preventing wider dissemination of nuclear weapons. Several other points were also raised. In the final analysis it was left to the two co-chairmen to decide what subject would be dealt with first.
The communists took exception to our proposal on outer space being considered first. They said that it should be considered in the main debate on a disarmament treaty and they raised some other technical objections. Our proposal received excellent support from Great Britain, Italy, Mexico, Sweden and India, and I think all the eight non-aligned countries and the United States would like to have this subject discussed; the question remains whether we can succeed in having it discussed first in this special committee. It will be discussed at some time, but I am not sure at what stage that will be.

Another feature of the organization is this. There is a subcommittee on a nuclear test ban set up by the conference comprising the three nuclear powers, the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet union. They have been meeting but as yet have reached no agreement. The big obstacle is the question of verification. They are still meeting and may be reporting to the plenary today. We suggested that some of the non-aligned countries be added to the subcommittee of three. That suggestion has not yet been taken up and indeed it may not be, but in any event the non-aligned countries will be drawn into the picture in one way or another.
Arrangements have also been made for informal meetings of the conference, and we have had several already. No record is kept, and there are only three present from each country. You can ask questions, talk across the table and let your hair down to a degree that you cannot in a plenary meeting. This, I believe, is an entirely new feature in disarmament negotiations, and I think a very helpful one.
The atmosphere of the conference to date has been one of moderation. No delegates have made nasty speeches, though some have leaned a bit that way. Generally speaking, however, the statements have been constructive, and I think this is probably one of the outstanding features of the whole conference.
In the early days of the conference general statements were made by representatives of each of the 17 nations. Unfortunately France is not represented, although there is a chair there for her. I believe that the opening statement made by Canada has either been tabled or printed in Hansard so I will not go over it today, but our main purpose was to pinpoint subjects on which there was near agreement between the United States and the Soviet union. There are quite a few of these subjects where it would not take a great deal for the two sides to get together. We believe it is of great importance to stress these first, and this is what we will be doing as the conference proceeds.
In addition, of course, there have been many private talks between the different delegations. Mr. Rusk, Mr. Gromyko and Lord Home have had many such talks. Canada has also had many. We discussed the situation with the representatives of each of the other countries attending the conference, and I think these talks are very useful. They afford a foreign minister an opportunity as well to discuss any subject in which another country represented at the conference is involved. Mind you, I think all the foreign ministers have left now, or they will all be gone by tomorrow. They are like a lot of seagulls;

Geneva Disarmament Conference when one goes all the rest go, and you are considered a bit of a scab if you stay around after the rest have gone. I found it safer to go home at that particular stage. However, the Canadian delegation is in exceedingly good hands under Lieutenant General E. L. M. Burns, who in my opinion is the outstanding expert on disarmament in the world today and who certainly has the respect of the members of all the other delegations.
For a couple of days before the conference met and while it was meeting there were discussions on the question of Berlin among the Americans, the Russians and the British. No one could be expected to solve the Berlin question in a matter of two or three days, but because it was not solved in these talks there has been quite a lot of pessimistic reporting, particularly in United States newspapers. They got the talks on Berlin all mixed up with the disarmament conference, and some of them reported right from the start that the disarmament conference was doomed, that it had been a failure before it began and all that sort of nonsense. That was not a very helpful attitude for those who were trying to get some results in the disarmament conference. Before Mr. Rusk left last Tuesday he and Mr. Gromyko issued a joint statement concerning Berlin, in these words:
In connection with their presence in Geneva to attend the opening sessions of the 18 nation committee on disarmament, the foreign ministers of the U.S.S.R. and the United States have had a series of meetings devoted to a discussion of the German problem and related questions. Their conversations have been both useful and frank, and some progress has been made in clarifying points of agreement and points of difference. They have agreed to resume contact in an appropriate way after reporting to their respective governments and after consultation with their allies.
It is of great significance that these two men, who today carry tremendous loads in world affairs, had the opportunity for over two weeks to meet and consider these issues and discuss them thoroughly. That, I think, has been of great importance. Mr. Rusk said goodbye to Mr. Gromyko at a luncheon I gave, and they parted on the understanding that they would keep in touch with each other.
I become annoyed with this attitude of hopelessness, that nothing can be done, that the world is going to the dogs, that we are all going to be blown up and we might just as well do nothing and get blown up. That does not make much sense to me and I do not think it does to a lot of other people because, for one thing, we do not want to be blown up. I think the leaders of the world today have a responsibility to see that this great tragedy, this tragedy to end all tragedies, does not occur. I cannot promise anything, but I am hopeful and there is no


reason why agreement should not be reached fairly quickly on some of the points.
I am prepared to go back to Geneva at any time provided some of the other foreign ministers return, and if progress is made I think there is a possibility that the heads of state will meet. They could then give the conference further impetus and probably reach agreement on subjects on which the foreign ministers and the other delegates have not been able to agree. The conference has begun very well. Canada will be doing her part to see that its deliberations are successful. The cause is a great one, and we are in a good position in the conference. We are on good terms with everybody, and I know I have the support of the house when I say that Canada at least will do her full part to restore sanity in this fear riddled world.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the eve of his departure for Geneva I had the pleasure of extending to the hon. gentleman the good wishes of the house. As the first spokesman today for the opposition, I have the pleasure of welcoming him back to the house. The minister seems to have performed a useful service in outlining to his colleagues at the conference of 17 powers the desirability of noting areas of agreement, particularly among the Soviet union, the United States and the United Kingdom. The minister said that one notable achievement seemed to be the possibility of agreement between the Soviet union and other interested powers on a preamble which would be annexed of course, to an agreement on disarmament.

It is significant that if this is the measure of achievement, then we have an indication of the very great difficulty of arriving, in the foreseeable future, at a comprehensive agreement on disarmament.
The minister indicated that Canada had placed great stress on a declaration or prohibition against stationing nuclear weapon carriers in space. He did not say, but it has been reported, that such a ban would require an exchange of information on launchings. There would be no inspection services required in the sense in which that term has been used in other contexts in disarmament discussions. This would be by way of a declaration, and this is different, apparently, from what the United States wants, namely

that such a declaration should be transferred into an agreement in the form of a convention or treaty. It has been reported that while the eight unaligned states did support this Canadian position, the United States and the Soviet union did not seem to pay much attention to the suggestion and did not give it anything like the same kind of support.

The minister says he thinks it would include them all, but that is not what has been reported. Of course the minister is in a better position to say. This would mean, if there was a meeting of the heads of government, that instead of there being 17 foreign ministers in the guise of seagulls there would also be at least a similar number of prime ministers likewise in the the guise of seagulls, who would be flying from their countries some perhaps during a period of great intensification of activity.
The minister did not say anything about the cessation of tests, a problem which we know engages his interest and attention. The minister said nothing about the determination of the United States, as related yesterday by the President, to resume testing unless an agreement is forthcoming with the Soviet union in Geneva during the next few weeks. The minister is reported, however, as having said outside the conference that Canada's position with regard to tests was unchanged and, of course, that puts Canada in opposition to the position taken by the United States.

We hope to have an opportunity, Mr. Speaker, when the minister's estimates are before us to go into these matters in further detail. I may say to the minister that all members of the house share the view that any effort toward disarmament is one to which we must studiously direct our fullest attention. We are all agreed that we can remove one of the possible sources of war by miscalculation through an agreement on disarmament, in a manner which does not prejudice the security position of this or any other country concerned.
To the extent that my hon. friend, as spokesman for Canada, was able to make a contribution toward this objective, which in the light of existing difficulties seems to be a long way off, he may be assured that the house is with him as are indeed the people of the country, who want to see the elimination of these dangerous and mischievous instruments of war under circumstances that will not prejudice our security.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that we will have an opportunity to discuss external affairs in a few minutes, my comments will be quite brief. However, I must express on behalf of this group a most sincere and warm welcome to the minister on his return. We have followed the course of the conference at Geneva with close interest almost daily, and particularly the minister's efforts at that conference on behalf of peace. We admire his stubborn determination, regardless of the criticism that comes from some quarters, to be undismayed by temporary set-backs. The minister will not mind a sort of personal reference, I am sure, when I say that in the opinion of this group his self effacing, mule-like qualities are of value to Canada at this time and particularly to his office under these trying circumstances.
I was very interested in the minister's report. I have no hesitation in saying it was one of the best, most heartening reports in relation to world conditions we have heard a secretary of state for external affairs give in this house. We were most interested to hear about the arrangements for the appointment of co-chairmen. This is evidently a very worth-while step. I am one of those, and I think the minister would agree with me, who believe it is not always the legalistic approach that gains the objectives; it is getting human beings together across a table. I think the minister has had a good influence in that direction. We were interested also in hearing of the growing influence of the unaligned

countries. I think that is a helpful development and, from our point of view, Canada has taken a very worth-while stand in promoting that development.

I have great pleasure in announcing the final payment on wheat for the 1960-61 pool. This final payment is the largest of its kind in the history of the operation of the Canadian wheat board. It would not have been possible without accelerated sales to traditional markets, without sales guaranteed by government credit terms, and without the effect of the recent devaluation of the Canadian dollar.
As the Prime Minister reported on February 2 last, the pool account was closed on February 28, 1962. The final accounting has now been completed. Producers delivered 392.8 million bushels to the 1960-61 pool. The 1960-61 pool closed with a surplus of $165,500,284, including the interim payment of $39,282,601 paid to the producers during November last. The final distribution to producers will therefore amount to $125,088,385, after allowing for the Prairie Farm Assistance Act levy, the cost of issuing final payment cheques and after crediting the account with estimated additional interest earnings.
On producers' deliveries of 392,826,011 bushels, the average final payment is 31.843 cents per bushel. This compares with an average final payment on the 1959-60 pool account of 12.001 cents per bushel. Final payments for the principal grades of wheat delivered to the 1960-61 pool are as follows:

The Canadian wheat board will commence to issue the final payment cheques early in April. I might repeat, Mr. Speaker, that this final payment is the largest of its kind in the history of the operation of the Canadian wheat board. It comes at a time when, due to poor crops in 1961, prairie farm income would ordinarily have been at a very low level. Coupled with the adjustment payment on the 1961-62 pool that will follow in May, it is hoped that the main shock of last year's poor crop may have been met.

speechtext: This important announcement by the Minister of Agriculture is another demonstration of the very efficient operation of the Canadian wheat board. Even though hon. members opposite may laugh at this remark-

-the Canadian wheat board, which has been doing this work for so many years. The minister has announced what he described as the largest final payment ever made. However, I wish to point out that there was only one previous interim payment. This is the final payment, but this "largest final payment" is merely bringing the final price, the total price of wheat received by Canadian producers, back to a position comparable to but somewhat below the price received by the producers for wheat during the years following the second world war and, in context with the very severe increases in costs of production since 1945, the farmer still has a long way to go to the price-cost position at that time.
The total payments announced at this time do not mean that the Canadian wheat producer is receiving anything like special treatment. He is getting the world commercial price for wheat, without subsidy by the government, and with the Australian wheat producer he is still receiving the lowest price for wheat in the world. That is one factor that also must be considered.
The final payments on Durum were about what one might have expected, although I thought they might have been a few cents higher-just a few cents higher. As the price of Durum is very high today, I believe that the final price for Durum wheat sold during the present crop year will undoubtedly be considerably more than the total final payment for Durum which the minister has just announced.

The minister's statement once again demonstrates the wisdom of western grain producers in supporting the Canadian wheat board's system of orderly marketing.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On orders of the day:

subtopic: ADVERSE EFFECTS OF NEW DRUG ON PREGNANT WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether I could direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. My question is based on an article in this morning's Globe and Mail to the effect that a drug called thalidomide contributed to the birth to a Winnipeg woman of a malformed child. The article also states that on March 21 this drug was withdrawn from the Canadian market. My question is, inasmuch as the article indicates that there is still some quantity of the drug in existence, could the

minister indicate what steps are being taken, if any, to ensure that no further use is being made of this particular drug?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monteiih (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ADVERSE EFFECTS OF NEW DRUG ON PREGNANT WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to this drug known as thalidomide or kevadon, the new drug submission was cleared on November 22, 1960 and the drug was added to schedule F of the Food and Drugs Act, which meant that it was for prescription sale only. On April 1, 1961 this drug was introduced to the Canadian market after all the usual forms of testing and records had been received and studied, and so on.
On December 1, 1961 the medical representatives of the two companies manufacturing this drug came to Canada to inform us of reports of congenital malformations in newborn infants which had been reported from Germany following the use of thalidomide in pregnant women. The information supplied was statistical in nature, in that the instances of certain malformations in the group of children born to mothers taking the drug were somewhat higher than in a group of children from mothers not taking the drug. A warning letter was sent out to physicians, informing them of this fact, by the two companies concerned on December 4 and 5, 1961.
On March 2, 1962 the department decided that there was now sufficient evidence to warrant a request to the manufacturers that the drug be withdrawn entirely and the manufacturers were so informed on the same day by telephone and letter. A letter was also sent to all physicians on March 5, 1962. Efforts are being made, Mr. Speaker, to make sure that any drug still on the market is picked up.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee adjourned for lunch I was asking some questions in connection with the transfer of the Vancouver airport to the Department of Transport. I will not repeat what I asked because I am sure the parliamentary

secretary is ready to give a reply. However, there are one or two other questions that arise out of this matter.
During the course of his reply I trust that the parliamentary secretary will be in a position to say whether this agreement has been finalized with the city of Vancouver. I understand that under the municipal bylaws or regulations of that city, any agreement made with a federal department has to be approved of by vote; whether it be in the form of a plebiscite or a vote at a municipal election, I do not recall at the moment.
I would like to know, (1) what is the price of the sale or the transfer; (2) whether it has been approved of by the ratepayers of the city of Vancouver, and (3) whether that agreement is now finalized; in other words, is there a signed agreement which is effective between the department and the city of Vancouver?
Following the answers to those three questions perhaps we can enter into a discussion of this item.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had really intended to indicate the purpose of this item in the first instance, which is of course rather different than answering the questions which the hon. gentleman has asked. However, perhaps I might deal directly with the questions he has asked, which really apply to a transport item but I will be very glad to deal with them now.
First as to the price. The price which was agreed upon and appraised was $2,750,000, which was subject to a number of deductions for previous federal grants totalling $216,250, so the net price payable is $2,533,750.
The hon. gentleman is quite right in believing that it is required that there be the approval of the ratepayers of Vancouver, and I am told that this approval has now been given and the takeover date, which has been agreed upon, is the first day of June next. I assume that this is a bylaw approval in the usual way. My hon. friend and I are members of the Ontario bar, and I assume it is an approval of a bylaw in the same way that we would understand. As I say, agreement has been reached for a takeover date of June 1 and I am assured that all preparations to that effect are in progress.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Has the agreement been signed?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I am told that it has. I think the hon. gentleman would perhaps like to know what we are endeavouring to do by this item; that is, we are trying to bring the employees of the Vancouver airport into a position equivalent to that of a civil servant. There is no reciprocal agreement in respect of superannuation between the federal

government and the municipality of Vancouver. There are perhaps fewer reciprocal agreements in respect of superannuation matters than there ought to be generally across the country. Personally I would hope that reciprocal agreements might increase in number and give a greater fluidity of movement of public servants as among municipal, provincial and federal authorities.
The vote in this particular is similar to a vote which was adopted in respect of Quebec fishery inspectors when they were transferred,
I think in the year 1959. The vote will permit the recognition of the pensionable service of each employee on the same basis and to the same extent as if a reciprocal agreement had been included. Consequently, if the amount transferred in respect of a particular employee is insufficient to purchase the full past service credit, the employee will be permitted to contribute the balance of it and in the net result he will be put in the same position as if he had been a civil servant.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

My hon. friend said that the agreement had been signed between the Department of Transport and the city of Vancouver. Does the agreement cover the persons referred to under item 712 which we are now discussing; in other words, was a provision made in the agreement for taking over these employees as employees of the Department of Transport? Second, was a committee established to determine what benefits would flow to these employees of the municipality of Vancouver by becoming employees of the Department of Transport? I presume that these employees will now be in the same category as, for instance, employees at Dorval airport in Montreal or Malton airport in Toronto of the Department of Transport. I wonder whether the parliamentary secretary would answer those questions.

This figure is the result of a cumulative deficit of $17,271.25 as at January 31, 1961, plus an operating surplus of $9,395.67 for the 12 months ended January 31, 1962. An earlier deficit of $30,159 in this account had been recouped through estimates.
In the lobster trap account at January 31, 1962, the excess of indemnities over premiums stood at $79,907.92. Earlier deficits of $378,115.84 in this account had been recouped through estimates, $114,480 of it as recently as in further supplementary estimates (5), 1960-61.
The over-all fund covering both vessel and trap operations has a ceiling of $150,000, and the cumulative deficits of $7,875.58 in vessels and $79,907.92 in traps totalling $87,783.50 leave therefore only $62,216.50 at January 31, 1962 as a working margin against further abnormal losses.
At the end of January 1962 there were 6,010 vessels covered by the plan valued at $19,788,000, an increase of 377 vessels and $2,074,000 during the previous 12 months. The present maximum contingent liability is $13,240,000, an increase of $1,383,000 over the figure of one year ago.

My second point is this. I believe it is an awkward way to proceed, by way of a vote of parliament and subsequent statutory coverage, compared with the system of setting up a fund through a separate act.
The Prime Minister was concerned about the former system of appointing parliamentary secretaries and subsequently introduced a system under which parliamentary secretaries are appointed by authority of an act of parliament. In my opinion it would be better to deal with these matters by means of a statute

rather than by means of an estimate with subsequent action by the governor in council to establish regulations.
The system that has been in existence for many years amounts to giving the cabinet a blank cheque to proceed on whatever basis it likes and set up whatever funds it likes under the fisheries indemnities plan. Mr. Chairman, I wish to bring to the attention of the committee under this item a matter of serious concern to my constituents. I have been asked to raise it by numerous organizations including chambers of commerce, labour, industry, farm institutes, women's institutes and one Anglican bishop in my constituency who has a great sense of social responsibility. I refer to the recent bombings and burnings that have occurred in the district I have the honour to represent. This is a serious problem. These incidents have occurred since 1923 and according to a qualified official of Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company who has kept a record, the loss to date totals more than $17 million as a result of bombings and burnings, the blowing up of railroads and bridges, the destruction of community halls and houses, and so on. That means that to date the loss averages $1,200 a day. In addition there is an average annual expenditure by the provincial government of over $300,000.
In fairness to the greater body of Doukho-bors I should explain to the committee the distinction between the main body, the Sons of Freedom and the fanatical sect of the Sons of Freedom. I do this also for the members of the fourth estate, who are gentlemen, and others connected with that vocation. The Doukhobors in the interior of British Columbia number somewhere between 8,000 and 10,000 and are a hard working, law abiding group of citizens. Then we have the Sons of Freedom group which numbers between 2,000 and 2,500. These on the whole are also law abiding but in that group there is an unrepentant fanatical minority. It is difficult to estimate the number in this group but it is possibly somewhere between 200 and 300. It is the fanatical minority that has caused trouble throughout the years. I hope that hon. members of the committee and the
Supply-Justice
gentlemen of the fourth estate in future will not report these incidents as having been caused by the Doukhobors but will refer to them as the fanatical sect of the Sons of Freedom section.
The latest outrage that has caused considerable uproar in my constituency is the bombing of the power pylon-the largest over-water power line in the west-on the west shore of Kootenay lake causing damage estimated at $1 million which resulted in throwing out of employment approximately 1,000 miners and smelter workers and others associated with the mining and lumbering industries. Some may be out of work for several months, but it is hoped that the majority may be given employment as the weeks go by so the loss in terms of wages will be mitigated to some extent. This has caused strong feelings in the district I have the honour to represent together with the hon. member for Kootenay East who, I am certain, is burning to follow me in this debate because we co-operate in doing what we can in these situations.
Before proceeding I wish to compliment the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers and other unions in the district who have met with the employer, Consolidated Mining and various employers in the forest and other industries affected and have done their best to work out staggered hours of employment and rearrangement of activities so the loss will be lessened as far as planning to that extent can lessen it.
I have received wires, letters and resolutions from the Kootenay and boundary citizens committee on Canadian and Doukhobor affairs, from the mayors of municipalities, labour organizations, chambers of commerce, other groups and numerous individuals expressing their concern about this continuing situation and urging that certain steps be taken to remedy it.
First of all they have asked for the maintenance of law and order and requested that more members of the R.C.M.P. be made available in the district. I understand the minister made available additional members of the force from Alberta and to that extent the situation has been remedied. Naturally, those who are proved guilty must be punished and law and order must be maintained.
Second, various mayors and municipalities and other organizations have urged the sending of troops into the district by the Department of National Defence, not to be used against the unfortunate people who are being misled by certain leaders who in the past duped them out of large sums of money, but as a protection to all citizens including members of the Sons of Freedom group against

Supply-Justice
whom there was a large degree of resentment for a few days, as a protection for property and as a stabilizing influence.
I have raised this question in the house. The Minister of National Defence has taken a somewhat niggling point of view in suggesting that the attorney general should apply to the officer commanding in the area to see whether he can maintain law and order. That is not the purpose of this request. It is possible to have a company there in training available to protect property. That is their opinion. I am not suggesting it is a complete remedy to the situation. The people of the district cannot understand why it is not possible to train a battalion or company in the Kootenays. It is magnificent country for certain types of training such as mountain climbing, skiing, building bridges, swimming, and other water sports, and there are adequate unusual natural obstacles. The people cannot understand the position of the department, especially when they learn that the Department of National Defence is going to send 600 troops to the world's fair at Seattle for a week. Sending troops to the Kootenays will cost the taxpayers of Canada money, and if it is a matter of expense I cannot see the argument because these troops have to be paid and so on. In any event, that is a matter that is being decided between the Minister of National Defence and the attorney general of British Columbia, but I mention it because it has been brought to my attention by these organizations.
I have also had resolutions from various organizations, including the Kootenay and Boundary committee on Canadian and Doukhobor affairs, urging these matters and also suggesting that the losses suffered by corporations and individuals should be shared by the federal and provincial governments. I put that forward as another suggestion to those on the government side of the house who, I trust, are listening to my pleas.
Then there is the question of rehabilitation. A good number of people have written to me urging that consideration be given to the problem of rehabilitation. Mind you, this is the most difficult social problem in Canada related to one particular group. It is of the longest standing and is one of the most difficult ones. I know these people. I have talked to them. In fact, I am getting letters daily from some of them who are in jail. I had two this morning, one from one of the former leaders in which he explains the circumstances. He is not complaining and, as a matter of fact, seems quite happy, but he is giving me his views.
On the whole these are simple people who have been misled throughout the years and
[Mr. Herridge. j
who have been bled financially by some leaders. In the past governments have seen fit to pass the buck from one to the other. They have taken a purely legalistic view of the problem. The federal government has said on many occasions that the maintenance of law and order, property and civil rights, etc. are the responsibility of the provincial government.
I am trying to be as brief as possible, Mr. Chairman. I do not want to take the time of the committee unduly but this is a serious problem to the people I have the honour to represent.
It so happens that 10 years ago this month the consultative committee tabled its report on its research into the whole problem and it made some excellent recommendations. At that time the people of the Kootenays looked forward to co-operation between the federal and provincial governments toward a final solution of the problem, but nothing happened. I have some correspondence here. In 1950 the matter was discussed between the attorney general of the province at that time, Mr. G. S. Wismer, and Mr. Stuart Garson who was minister of justice, and the situation is described in the same terms as I am describing it today. But nothing happened.
I also have copies of an exchange of letters in 1953 between the Hon. Stuart S. Garson, Q.C., minister of justice and the Hon. R. W. Bonner, Q.C., attorney general of British Columbia, relating to the British Columbia Doukhobor problem. Once again may I say that I do not like the word "Doukhobor". "Doukhobor" is a Russian word meaning spirit wrestler. The matter should be referred to as the Sons of Freedom problem and I want to impress that on the authorities.
I wish to read briefly from one letter in the correspondence. One would judge that at that time the governments were co-operating very closely to meet the problem. Mr. Bonner wrote to Mr. Garson on May 20, 1953, and I quote part of the letter:
A complete solution to the problem posed by the Sons of Freedom sect of the Doukhobor community lies beyond the constitutional competence of the provincial government and requires the closest co-operation of the federal and provincial governments which jointly share the sum total of constitutional competence to deal with this problem. We ask, therefore, that the federal government recognize this basic position.
I am asking this federal government to do exactly that. Then Mr. Bonner went on to make several suggestions. I might say that I discussed this problem with Mr. Garson at some length because I have lived with it for over 40 years. Some of these people have worked on my ranch and when they are away from the influence of their community you could not have better or more industrious

workers or more kindly people. I know the whole circumstances. In any event, Mr. Garson to his credit did make an offer of co-operation. He discussed the question of relocation in the Slocan valley, the rebuilding of the communities and so on; but unfortunately Mr. Garson did not get a reply to his letter to the attorney general of British Columbia and the matter was left more or less in the air. Nothing was done. No action was taken in 1950; no action was taken in 1953.
What do I suggest? I suggest in broad outline the recommendations of the consultative committee on Doukhobor and Sons of Freedom affairs which made its report 10 years ago this month. First of all, I urge that the government abandon the strictly legalistic approach to the question and that they approach the government of British Columbia and offer their co-operation. Let them take the initial step and offer their co-operation in any way possible.
I suggest that what is required is a commission that can make a quick report. The basic facts are there. The consultative committee's report was the result of a great deal of research and it is the foundation upon which any later report could be made. First of all, federal-provincial co-operation is required and I suggest that the federal government offer to co-operate. Then a commission is required to make a quick examination of the problem, based on previous material which is available and on interviews with the people of the district. I suggest that the commission go to the Kootenays and meet representatives of the churches, labour, industry, the chambers of commerce and the farmers' and women's institutes. I am sure they will find that the representatives of these organizations and their members are willing to extend their co-operation and accept their responsibilities as organizations and individuals in working toward a solution. I suggest that after that committee reports there should be co-operation between both governments and the recommendations should be given effect as a result of co-operation between the governments, the organs of the people in the district concerned and the people.
I have had a lot of people write me who are most interested and concerned and there are many very capable persons available who could make a great contribution. I had a letter from a very well known bishop in my constituency just two days ago in which he deals with the whole question. He is a retired man of means, a man of outstanding intellect, and he knows these people. There is one man who would be able to serve on the committee and would make a great contribution because
Supply-Justice
of his contacts with the Sons of Freedom, the Doukhobor people and the balance of the community and because of the respect in which he is held by all communities. I am sure there are leading people in all the churches who could make a contribution in that respect. The country is simply alive with talented persons who are willing to do something if there is some mobilization of government forces and of the local people's capacity to meet the problem. I suggest that we should meet it head on.
We hear about immigration. I have a letter here from the Brazilian embassy. Some of the representatives of the Sons of Freedom, who now have written me to say they are in the penitentiary, went to Brazil and made arrangements to buy 5,000 acres of land; but the question of the Brazilian government permitting them to enter the country had to be considered. I received a letter dated March 8 from the charge d'affaires of the Brazilian embassy which reads as follows:
In reply to your letter dated March 7 concerning the Doukhobor question. I would like to advise you that the Brazilian government is still studying the request for the group to migrate to Brazil. As soon as I receive any information on this question, I will be very pleased to contact you.
I am not very hopeful in that respect, Mr. Chairman. I am sure that recent events would not cause any country to welcome some of these people with open arms. I think we have to face this question head on. We have other people who are suggesting that these Doukho-bors should be sent to other parts of Canada. As soon as you suggest that, the people in the other parts of Canada hold meetings of protest. While we have to punish the guilty and maintain law and order, we have civil rights in this country. I have heard people suggest that the whole group should be moved to some other part of Canada. However, we have a bill of rights and you cannot take a group of people who have not been proven guilty of any crime and move them to another part of Canada. This is against our bill of rights, our democratic principles and so on.
I say to our people in the Kootenays, let us face this question head on. You know, we have thousands of acres of good land there. We have a valley 30 miles long with a paved highway right through it and with electricity to light every farm. We have a large river flowing through this valley. This land would provide the opportunity for resettlement, reeducation, vocational training and social rehabilitation. What we require is co-operation between the federal and provincial governments and then co-operation between agencies such as the P.F.R.A., the Veterans Land Act administration, the Farm Credit Corporation and the provincial agencies directly concerned.

Supply-Justice
I might say that when I discussed this matter with Mr. Garson, he was prepared to recommend to the cabinet that we go along with such a scheme as that, utilizing the P.F.R.A. At that time I suggested these people be resettled, re-educated and sent to vocational training schools. There are some bright aspects of this problem, regardless of this recent catastrophe which resulted in the destruction of this pylon and the damage that flowed therefrom. However, the young Douk-hobor women, the Sons of Freedom women, have continued to send their children to school. These are the young women who could have a big influence in the future with regard to the community, and they are the persons with whom our organizations should be dealing. I suggest that having the land, the roads, the power, the public facilities and the capacity in the district, we should mobilize all these forces. I suggest the government could rebuild the jam factory. You know, the finest jam in the country was manufactured by the Doukhobors in this area. Do you know why it was the finest? It was the finest because nothing but plain sugar and the finest fruit were used. There was no jiggery-pokery about it like there is with a lot of monopoly capitalism. This jam was known throughout the whole country and they could not supply the demand. I have been in the factory many times. I think government action through these various agencies could rehabilitate these people. I say let us face it together; let us work at it together and give the local people an opportunity to do something as the result of government action.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I have tried to be as brief as possible on a question of great importance to my constituents. I do urge this government to offer its co-operation to the provincial government in an effort to find a long term solution to this problem. Let both governments work together with the people of the Koote-nays and let us accept this challenge in the spirit that we intend to succeed and end for all time this social disability.

Mr. Chairman, this is one of the rare occasions in this House of Commons upon which members of opposing political parties join hands for the benefit of the people in general. I certainly agree with many of the remarks that have been made by the hon. member for Kootenay West. During a period of many years-I am going back now about 40 years-we have had similar conditions in the Kootenays but not quite so serious as the recent outbreak. I have had a certain amount of personal contact with many of the Sons of Freedom sect, as we call them, and generally speaking I have found them to be very good people.

They have been actively concerned with local civic projects and the average member of the sect has been a credit to the district in which he has lived. Of course, you will find radicals in any organization or in any group of people.
I have also received wires and letters from the chambers of commerce, cities and villages in the area. I will eliminate the women's institutes in the area because I think they have other things to consider. The latest bombing has affected part of my area. Not long ago we had a grain elevator blown up twice and this radical sect also endeavoured to blow up a little church in this area. It was fortunate that the time bomb did not go off. The men who were sent in to defuse the bomb had to be very careful, but they were able to eliminate this danger without too much difficulty. This latest bombing is something that has affected my area. It has thrown a considerable number of men out of work as the result of the closure of the fertilizer plant and the iron plant, which were working to full capacity at this time of the year. Electrical power, which we need in the area, was reduced to the point where it was barely sufficient to carry on the essentials.
Prior to this time, and over a period of 40 years, we have experienced many of these bombings and possibly we have treated them a little too lightly. We have accepted them as a matter of course. It was nothing to pick up the paper in the morning and find that the Sons of Freedom had blown up part of the railway track or a power pole. We did not take the matter too seriously. It was not a major subject of conversation. The situation has reached the point now, Mr. Chairman, where something must be done. We cannot go along living in danger of our power plants being destroyed, our theatres blown up or places of business destroyed with a possible resultant loss of life. Something must be done now.
It has been said that the provincial authorities neglected to request help at the time they should have asked for it. As soon as the extent of this bombing was known, a wire or telephone call from the provincial authorities should have been made requesting the proper assistance. I should like to read from Hansard, page 1593, March 8, 1962. A question was asked of the Minister of National Defence, and he replied as follows:
The responsibility for maintaining law and order in the Kootenays, as indicated by the Minister of Justice, is with the provincial authorities. It would appear to me that until they have exhausted their capabilities in that direction there would be no necessity to call upon the members of the Canadian army to assist them in that regard.

The point I want to bring out, Mr. Chairman, is that the provincial authorities did not accept their responsibility and request assistance from the federal government which, we have been assured, would have been supplied. In closing, Mr. Chairman, I would say that we must have the co-operation, of the federal and provincial governments as well as the small municipalities concerned in order to bring this matter to a satisfactory conclusion.

I fully appreciate the contribution made by the hon. member for Kootenay West and the hon. member for Kootenay East on the Doukhobor question. However my purpose in rising is entirely different and I would like to restrict my remarks to the item under discussion.
On studying these estimates, I find that according to page 18 the government is asking for a sum of $5,000 to cover travelling and living expenses for the committee on juvenile delinquency. I do want to deal at length with that item because it was the subject of discussion the other day and was fully ventilated. However the government is asking for a further amount of $75,500; but on examining pages 239 and 240 of the blue book I find these special sub-items dealing with professional and special services, travelling expenses, telephones, telegrams, publications, departmental reports and other matters, amount to a total of $180,000. Therefore this further amount represents over 60 per cent of the original estimate.
To me that is a tremendous amount of money by comparison with the original estimate, and there must be good reasons for it. Offhand I cannot discover any and I wonder is it due to lack of foresight on the part of the department, or what special reasons have brought it about. I ask the parliamentary secretary why these further amounts are required? Is it due to lack of foresight, or what?
I have a special interest in the last amount which deals with publication of departmental reports and other material. The original estimate seeks $2,500 but this last supplementary is asking for $15,700. That is an increase of over 600 per cent. I find it hard to understand and I would like the parliamentary secretary to explain why that amount is required.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words only on this item, following the question I put this morning to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), on the orders of the day, when I asked him whether the government had sent an observer to the inquiry on organized crime in Ontario.
Supply-Justice
The minister seemed rather surprised at my question. I must say I was much more surprised at the reply he gave me. The Minister of Justice has taken the ridiculous position that, since it is a case of a provincial inquiry on organized crime, we should keep aloof from it to respect provincial autonomy.
That a minister of justice should take a certain position for sound reasons, that is his own responsibility; but to justify on such childish grounds the absence of a departmental observer in so serious a matter as the royal commission on organized crime in Ontario, I say is inconceivable.
The minister is then of the opinion that organized crime knows frontiers in Canada. Nothing is more contrary to the facts, and all those who have any experience in the matter will find that the argument of the Minister of Justice does not make sense.
Crime, especially organized crime, knows no provincial frontiers, especially when we know that the inquiry on crime in the province of Ontario has been decided on account of the infiltration from the United States.
I submit it was the responsibility of the government, and especially of the Department of Justice, to be represented by an observer.
Mr. Chairman, I shall be very brief. But I do not want to leave on the record the impression which might have been created this morning by the reply given to my question by the Minister of Justice, because, at the time, on the orders of the day, the rules forbade me to do so.
Surely the Minister of Justice is not trying to make us believe that just by reading press reports he will have all the information and that he will be posted on the extent of the activities of organized crime, as uncovered by the inquiry. Coming as it does from people who have so often complained in the past three or four years that they are misquoted by the press, that statement is even more fantastic. Now they are saying: "Well, we will rely on press reports". We know very well that in a matter of this kind, newspaper accounts are necessarily incomplete since the press cannot give all the information an observer would be able to pick up if he were present.
All those who are interested in this matter -and they are much more numerous in Canada than one might think-feel that major amendments should be made to the Criminal Code in that regard. They will deplore not only that there is no observer at the inquiry but especially the apparent lack of interest which the Minister of Justice shows concerning that inquiry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have just two or three comments to make. Naturally all of us were interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West and the hon. member for Kootenay East in respect of the very difficult problem which exists in their area. Of course it is not a new problem. I well remember sitting as an observer in the gallery listening to a man who was a dear old friend of mine, Billy Esling, then member for Kootenay West describing the situation as it existed long years ago. Most regrettably it has not been possible to solve the problem that has existed since these people emigrated to Canada.
The remarks made by the two hon. gentlemen will be carefully noted, but I may say that the same representations made to them by public bodies have also been made directly to the Minister of Justice and the government generally. I can tell them the government remains ready, willing and anxious to cooperate with the provincial government of British Columbia and the local bodies in bringing a sane and rational solution to what is a really difficult problem.
The hon. gentleman from Megantic asked a number of questions in respect of this particular item. From the details given he will observe that professional and special services have increased, principally due to an unusual number of prosecutions of counterfeit cases in the province of Quebec.
Travelling expenses have also increased and this has been due to a need for travel which was not contemplated at the time. I may give an example of one of the items before me. It relates to the travelling expenses of an officer of the department while attending a United Nations consultative group on the prevention of crime and the treatment of offenders, which met in Geneva, Switzerland. The hon. gentleman himself mentioned the item of $5,000 which applies to the special departmental committee on juvenile delinquency which the Minister of Justice has established.
The item for telephone and telegraphs was underestimated having regard to last year's full expenditure for this item, which was in fact $18,359. This undoubtedly was an underestimation having regard to previous experience.
In the matter of the publication of departmental reports and other material, the department, as I think the hon. gentleman knows, has found it desirable to publish four
[Mr. Deschatelets.l
pamphlets which outline and cover the various functions of the Department of Justice. I am sure these pamphlets will be useful and that they will meet with the approval of the hon. gentleman.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont has raised again the question which he raised earlier in the day. As to the matters which were then in issue between himself and the Minister of Justice, I do not seek to intervene. I can assure the hon. gentleman that all aspects of any evidence which may be presented to any commission which relates to the enforcement of law under the jurisdiction of the federal government will be most carefully considered by the Minister of Justice and by the officials of the Department of Justice.
With regard to the question of the correct technique, the hon. gentleman appears to believe that it is wise for counsel on behalf of the dominion government to appear before provincial royal commissions. If that is his opinion, as I think it is, he is entitled to it. However, I suggest there are other techniques whereby the same objective can be achieved without an intervention on the part of the federal government in royal commissions which may be appointed by the provinces. I am sure the hon. gentleman and the Minister of Justice will have another occasion on which they can discuss this matter, and in such argument as they may put forward I would not seek to intervene.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, I would not like this item to be carried without reminding the parliamentary secretary that I did not mention or suggest any intervention; I just suggested that an observer should go there and report to the Minister of Justice here. Also, the minister in his reply this morning made it very clear that his only interest in this matter is in the reading of papers. I have no doubt whatsoever that the minister is able to read. Has he got time to read fully? I do not know. Do these newspaper reports cover all the field of the inquiry? I am sure that this question is answered in the negative. Therefore the answer just given by the parliamentary secretary does not meet the point I made; but I am very hopeful that one of these days the Minister of Justice will be able to answer adequately the suggestion I have made.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, of course the hon. gentleman appreciates that the enforcement of the Criminal Code is under the jurisdiction of the provincial attorneys general. I believe that the provincial attorneys general will do their duty in the enforcement of the code. If there should come

to the attention, through reading, listening or otherwise, anything wherein the Department of Justice can help in the proper enforcement of the law, my hon. friend can be assured that it will be done.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say just a word. I am really rising to say a word about what was said by the two hon. members from Kootenay, and it will be a very brief one I assure the parliamentary secretary.
Before doing that, in view of what has just been said I must say that the attitude of the Minister of Justice this morning and the parliamentary secretary this afternoon is very astonishing to me. That having an observer at a provincial royal commission should be an intervention in provincial affairs is certainly a new and strange doctrine in this country. After all, hon. gentlemen were just recently criticizing the premier and provincial treasurer of British Columbia because he did not appear before a federal royal commission on banking and commerce, which is exclusively under federal jurisdiction; and this government recently called a conference on a matter that is of purely provincial concern and took great exception because the premier of Quebec did not send a representative to it. In the light of those precedents-and I could mention a good many others-it does seem to me an attitude on the part of the government of straining at a gnat after it had swallowed, as the little girl once said, a saw mill.
It is not that about which I rose to speak, but I just could not resist saying a word about how really silly the Minister of Justice had been this morning. I do not blame the parliamentary secretary; he just had to repeat what the minister had said, because that is party solidarity. The parliamentary secretary would not have made such a ridiculous observation on his own. But I did rise to say just one word on and join with the hon. member for Kootenay West in the plea that everybody who refers to this unhappy and regrettable problem in the Kootenays should make a clear distinction between those people who are involved and the great body of Doukhobors who are descendants of the people who came to Canada in 1898, most of whom are just as good, law-abiding citizens of Canada as any other citizens of Canada and whose feelings must be injured every time these loose references are made. I do not criticize people too much for making them because most people are not as familiar with the problem as are the hon. gentlemen who spoke about it. Most people are not familiar enough with the problem to make that kind of distinction, but as it has been brought
Supply-Justice
to our attention I think it would be very desirable that we should make this distinction.
I also feel, like the hon. member for Kootenay West, that it is rather unfortunate- and I do not want to be unnecessarily critical about this-that the rather narrow and legalistic view was taken by the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Justice regarding the request of the attorney general and the premier of British Columbia. I have not any great admiration for the government of British Columbia, any more than has any other hon. member of this house that I know of, but I do think that the suggestion made by Mr. Bonner in this instance was a very sensible one indeed.
When you think of the tremendous amount of money we are spending on defence in this country it does seem to me that to have a small group of troops engaged in that area in some useful exercise might have had the very salutary moral effect that Mr. Bonner was hoping it might have, without having the invidious suggestion the troops were called in because the police could not do their job. I think it would have been the part of statesmanship on the part of the government of Canada to accept that suggestion in the broad spirit in which it was made and I rather regret what I think was a rather hasty and snap judgment.
I do not blame the federal government very much for being rather touchy and irritable about the government of British Columbia; heaven knows they have had to endure an awful lot of humiliation of one kind and another from them, including the absence of the Minister of Finance at the present time. Notwithstanding that fact, even the attorney general of British Columbia can occasionally be right about something, and in this instance it seems to me that he was right and was taking a broad view of this matter, and it is rather unfortunate that the government of Canada did not join with him in taking that view.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I only want to make one comment. If I thought that anyone in the committee would take seriously the use of the word "silly" in relation to any comment which has been made by the Minister of Justice, I would intervene further in the debate. The reason why I refrain from doing so is obvious.

Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary secretary speaks for himself. The Minister of Justice, like the rest of us, is quite capable of being silly at times, and quite often more silly than some of the rest of us.

715.	Administration of justice in the Northwest Territories, including the Northwest Territories territorial court-further amount required, $47,000.
(Translation):

(Text):

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, the first item, as the hon. gentleman from Megantic realizes, involves legal fees, court costs and payment for the maintenance of prisoners and juvenile delinquents in the Northwest Territories. An amount of $65,000 was included in the main estimates for these purposes and an additional $35,000 is required. As the hon. member, with his career at the bar, knows, it is a difficult matter to estimate from one year to the other what costs may be incurred in court fees and the maintenance of prisoners. There was an additional amount in respect of travelling expenses to members of the territorial court and the court staff while the court was on circuit. Much of this travelling was done by chartered aircraft and involved distances between places such as Yellowknife and Frobisher Bay and intermediate points. There was an underestimation of the amount required.

speakerposition: stagedirection

Yukon Territory-
716.	Administation of justice in the Yukon Territory, including the Yukon territorial court- further amount required, $41,000.

This item has to do with the Bankruptcy Act. Before I continue I should like to put a formal question to the parliamentary secretary. Does he know when the bill to amend the Bankruptcy Act will be introduced in the house? Will it be before dissolution? In the further supplementary last year, the parliamentary secretary may remember there was an amount of $52,000, I believe, having to do with special inquiries in relation to the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act, in the Montreal district particularly. These inquiries concerned trustees and I suppose this item represents an additional amount to cover expenditure of this kind.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
It is seldom that the hon. gentleman asks a loaded question, but
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
his first question was definitely a loaded one and I think he will forgive me if I do not reply to it, except to say that I am not in a position to inform the committee when a revised and consolidated Bankruptcy Act may be presented to parliament.
The hon. member is quite right with respect to the second matter he raised. This is the result of investigations into the administration of bankruptcy trustees in the province of Quebec and also in the province of Ontario. This investigation has resulted in the cancellation of the licences of several trustees and in some cases criminal prosecutions have been instituted. In dealing with this situation it has been found necessary to obtain legal advice, retain the services of the solicitors and so on. Accountants have been required to audit the books and to testify in the courts when necessary. With the authority of treasury board, the superintendent of bankruptcy entered into an arrangement to subsidize the work of a trustee in bankruptcy in Montreal to enable him to take over approximately 280 estates which were previously being handled by two trustees whose licences were cancelled.

I wish to thank the parliamentary secretary for that information. I am sure the trustee in Montreal, whom I know personally, will be able to handle those cases effectively.
I realize my first question was loaded but I refrained from putting it to the Minister of Justice earlier this afternoon on the orders of the day because I thought I would have the opportunity to ask the question on these estimates. However, I suppose I shall have to ask the question on the orders of the day on some other occasion.

I wish briefly to comment on this item. I must say we had hoped that the government would have introduced amendments to the Bankruptcy Act before this because the need is obvious and urgent from my point of view and from the point of view of a good many of the people I represent.
We have had citizens and companies from the United States coming into the district- I can speak of one man, and I can mention his name, because he is a rogue, a man named Pidge. He comes in and fleeces people of half a million dollars and then goes bankrupt. He does not pay wages; he does not pay for supplies; he does not pay income tax; he does not pay provincial taxes; he does not pay unemployment insurance contributions and he does not pay workmen's compensation. He goes bankrupt and clears off, leaving the employees and the tradesmen holding the bag.

There should be a strengthening of our bankruptcy laws to avoid any repetition of conduct of this kind.
Recently I heard that this bloke was coming back. I went to our immigration officer and said: "Do you have to let that bird into the country again?" He said: "Mr. Herridge, if he comes to the border and asks for admission I shall have to admit him. We all know he is a swindler but he has committed no crime in the ordinary sense of the word; he went bankrupt in the usual way and he can come back into the country." This kind of thing is happening all over the interior. There have been numerous instances, one just over three months ago. I hope there will be amendments to the Bankruptcy Act and to the Immigration Act which will net these birds before they come into our country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Without necessarily agreeing with the hon. gentleman as to his assessment of any particular individual, of whom I know nothing, I should like to say that the comments which he has made on this and earlier occasions have been duly noted.

I see the Minister of Justice is now in his place. I am glad to have an opportunity to ask him the question which I put earlier to the parliamentary secretary. Is the minister able to tell us when he expects to bring down a bill to amend the Bankruptcy Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the principle is well established that questions of this sort are not in order on supplementary estimates and that if asked they are not answered.
