speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on behalf of this group I wish to take advantage of the opportunity afforded by this item-
What group is that? Look behind you.

The unseen hosts surround me. I wish to take the last opportunity of this session to express our appreciation of the good work our Speaker has done, and his courtesy, and to express appreciation of the splendid services of Mr. Deputy Speaker and the Deputy Chairman of committees, and the house staff, the Clerk, the Clerk Assistant-I consider them the rubies surrounding the Speaker's crown, as it were-and the reporters and the Hansard angels. I include also the protective staff which is the nearest thing we have to a metropolitan police force in Canada-magnificent physical specimens, good looking, courteous, well informed and efficient -and the messengers and the elevator operators who provide valuable service every day, and even the cleaning ladies. Without these services we could not carry on the work of parliament and I think we as members of parliament should recognize this and express our appreciation.
I have had an idea in mind for some time. I think we in a fitting way should do something so that the lady members of the house will go down in posterity and be remembered far into the future. I got an inspiration the other day I wish to share with the committee. A creative member of the staff of the parliamentary restaurant has come up with an exciting creation called cream of chicken soup Judy. I feel this is one way in which we as members of parliament may ensure that the hon. ladies among us will be remembered for all time. If we could name dishes for them in the parliamentary restaurant their names

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys would go down in history. For instance, we could have haggis Margaret Macdonald and Jean's angel cake and Margaret's Formosa chow chow. But the women who are elevated to cabinet rank should receive special attention and I would suggest that the breakfast menu be left for them. What better way to recognize the splendid contribution the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has made to the development of the country than by having our breakfast menu headed in the future, "start the day with Ellen's mess of pottage". I just put this suggestion forward as a suitable way of commemorating our lady members, and although the suggestion is rather novel I trust it will commend itself to all hon. members.

General-
723.	Polar continental shelf project-further amount required, $103,565.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the parliamentary secretary should tell us who now has the contract for the helicopter work on the polar continental shelf, whether or not this contract was obtained by tender or by submitting tariffs to the board of transport commissioners, what the amount of the contract is and what is the total amount that it is expected will be expended on the polar continental shelf for this purpose.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Perhaps I might give the committee an indication of the nature of this item. This supplementary estimate, as the committee sees, is for $103,565. It is to provide for expenses arising out of the planned field program for 1962 and as my hon. friend well knows, because of climate, the program must commence in March of each year. In viewing the main estimates for 196162 the decrease in the vote of $100,000 was made on the understanding that the board might be prepared to approve a supplementary estimate should it be impossible because of the reduction to maintain the planned program. This is what has happened and it has been necessary, really, to reinstate the amount.
My hon. friend asks me the name of the present contractor. In respect of this I am advised that there is no general contract. There may be some subordinate contracts. This is a field program. I am sorry that that is all the information which I am in a position to give the hon. gentleman at the moment. I shall try to obtain some additional information.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Having listened carefully to what the parliamentary secretary said, in
(Mr. Herridge.]
the breakdown of the vote it is quite clear this has to do with the contract work in the polar continental shelf and since it has to do particularly with the planned field program which cannot be carried out unless there is helicopter service, I think the committee is entitled to know who the contractor is.
I understand that pursuant to the practice that has been adopted since this government has been in office a contract has been awarded-this I saw in the press-for the polar continental shelf fairly recently. This is for helicopter services. I think the committee is entitled to know who the contractor is, the amount of the contract and how it was awarded.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am advised that no contract has been let in respect of this.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Can the parliamentary secretary tell me who held the contract last year for helicopter services in the polar continental shelf?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes. They were friends of the hon. gentleman, Autair.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. I thank the parliamentary secretary very much for that information and for the adjective he used in describing my relationship with the company. Do I take it that this answer means that Autair Helicopter Services now have the contract for the 1962 services provided on the shelf only?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am informed that a letter of intent has been issued covering the services of Autair from March, 1962, until approximately August, 1962.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: For how much?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Approximately $275,000.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Does that cover the period for the whole services to be performed on the continental shelf?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Could the parliamentary
secretary tell me how the letter of intent was given? Was it given pursuant to a demand for tenders in the usual way?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
My information is that the normal action is to ask certain companies, certified by the air transport board as being competent in this field, for tenders of services. In this particular case all the major companies were asked to indicate their tenders of services. That having been done, an assessment is made in the department of the total cost likely to be encountered by the government. The hon. gentleman will know, of course, that with this vast area to be covered

the location of the helicopters is very important and that there are many complex factors to be considered. On the basis of the assessment which was made of economy and efficiency, the letter of intent of which I have spoken earlier was issued.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Could I obtain from the parliamentary assistant what other contracts this company received in the past? For instance, my hon. friend has told me that for the period March, 1962 to August, 1962, a letter of intent has gone out for a contract covering services in the amount of $275,000. What was the period in the year 1961 and what was the amount? What was the period in the year 1960 and what was the amount?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member will appreciate that the figures I am about to give are approximate only. In 1961 the amount was approximately $231,000 covering a period extending roughly from March to August, and in 1960 the amount was $170,000 for approximately the same period.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have just totalled these amounts and if the amounts given by the parliamentary secretary are correct the total is $676,000, close to $700,000. I take it that covers all of the contracts that have been awarded to this company. There are none prior to 1960, are there?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That covers all of them for this project.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The question that comes to my mind at once is this. A moment ago the parliamentary secretary stated what the normal action was in the tendering of these services. Does it appear normal to him that it is always the same company that obtains the work notwithstanding the fact that all companies have been asked to tender in connection therewith? Has the parliamentary secretary any comment on that point?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The only comment I would make is that location is a very big factor in relation to this matter, and it is my understanding that the department has been satisfied generally with the services that have been rendered. There are two aircraft positions in Resolute bay which constitute a very important factor and perhaps a capacity to give expeditious and efficient service in relation to the project.
The fact that this company possibly does not commend itself entirely to some members of the house does not necessarily indicate that it has not done an efficient and competent job in the work that has been undertaken.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
On that point may I say that I had not entered into that argument at all. However, the parliamentary secretary has

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys brought it up and I would remind him that when the company applied to the air transport board for a licence the board turned it down and decided against it in a formal judgment. It was only on appeal to the minister that the decision of the air transport board was reversed. I mention that only because the parliamentary secretary brought up the matter.
The point in which I am interested is the manner in which these submissions are obtained. Because of the method by which this is being done I am not satisfied in my own mind that the companies to whom offers of submission are sent are given a fair opportunity to submit a price that is acceptable to the department, and I would remind the parliamentary secretary that though there are not many there are certainly several helicopter companies in our country that can do this work efficiently. These companies have done similar work before elsewhere, have done it before on the polar continental shelf and are equipped so to do. What I am saying is that if the submission is one which asks the various companies to submit tenders, and they do, and an assessment is made by the departmental officials of what the costs are likely to be in the manner in which the former minister of mines and technical surveys made it, then, as I stated in the house before, that is not the acceptance of a tender. It is simply handing out a contract to one rather than another helicopter company. Along that line I would ask the parliamentary secretary to inform the committee as to the date of the letter of intent which gave this company the contract for the March-August, 1962 period.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: March 2, 1962.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few observations about this matter, and since this is precisely the same item as we had in supplementary estimates No. 3 I would draw the parliamentary secretary's attention to what was said by the minister, whose absence at the moment is conspicuous, about this very matter. As found on page 2028 of Hansard for March 21, I asked the minister whether this company had a contract and this was his reply:
The only thing I can say is that I have no information that it has anything to do with the $16,400 mentioned in this item.
That is no doubt correct or probably correct.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is correct.

I am not questioning that particular statement. Then I said:
The minister surely knows whether they have a contract. They might carry the materials to build this building. They might have something to do with it. Can the minister say whether they have a contract at the present time?
2362	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Do you mean in a field other than the one governed by this item?
In the continental shell program.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
I do not know. I would have to check. I am not in a position to give an answer now. I think this question was fully discussed last year. Perhaps a rereading of Hansard when the main estimates were discussed would provide an answer.
The minister told us this letter went on March 2. As the parliamentary secretary knows, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys was the product of that great cabinet reshuffle, that took place on December 29. He had been in the department for two months and he had been in the house, as his answer here indicates, during the previous debate that had taken place in connection with Autair. He knew that this was not a routine matter or he ought to have known it. I wish the minister were here because I am not seeking to use, in his absence, extreme language. It does seem to me that for the minister to say on March 21, having given a letter of intent on March 2, when he is asked whether or not these people have a contract-I am sure that the parliamentary secretary would not want to quibble about the difference between a letter of intent and a contract or indulge in that kind of sophistry-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would not agree that was sophistry.

The minister says:
I do not know. I would have to check. I am not in a position to give an answer now.
He either did know or he did not. If he wanted to say that a letter of intent was not a contract, he should have said, no, they have not a contract. This would have been a misleading answer, but literally a correct one. On the other hand, he could have said, yes, they have what is in effect a contract; they have a letter of intent. We know from experience with this company that if they get a letter of intent it is not revoked. This has not been the experience of some other companies in this field who have sought to get business from this government.
It seems to me, sir, that is a shocking thing for the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to have done on supplementary estimates No. 3. He ought to be here now to explain these estimates to the committee. Certainly, this company, with its very questionable past, this company that was rejected by an independent tribunal set up to consider the matter, as my hon. friend has just pointed out, should not be preferred over all others. Then, the minister sought by a statement that is a good deal less than frank to give the impression that nothing had been done about


this company. If you go on, sir, to read the next few exchanges, you will see that is what he did. He said:
Perhaps a rereading of Hansard when the main estimates were discussed would provide an answer.
At that point I said:
That might well be. But before the item passes- I do not want to delay it-may I express the hope, since we have a new minister, that the new minister is not as much associated with the past as some other ministers may have been. If he has any contracts to let for air services to the north may we hope that proper, competitive tenders will be called and that all competing companies will be allowed to compete for the business.
Here is the minister's reply:
I will give an assurance to the hon. member that my department will always proceed in this respect on the basis most economic for the department. But I am sure he will not quarrel with me if I do not go further at this time, because the whole system of asking for tenders in this field is not as simple as in other departments.
I think that my retort to that is rather eloquent:
We have found that out already.
I say this is an outrageous way for a suppliant government to be treating the committee of supply. The minister is not doing the job in his department; if he let the deputy or someone else give this letter of intent without telling him about it, he does not deserve to be minister. If he knew of that letter of intent and did not tell the committee about it in the face of these questions, it seems to me that he does not deserve the confidence of the house. It is conduct that is not becoming a member of the ministry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member has used extravagant language-
Quite the contrary.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
-in relation to this, and I think when he has time to consider he may perhaps wish to modify it somewhat. The fact is the answer of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys was completely accurate. The same statement could be made today. Autair, as of this hour, do not have a contract. A letter of intent was entered into and the formal terms of the contract, I am advised, are under negotiation at the present time. The statement which the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys made and which has been read to the committee by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate stands. He said, and I quote:
-my department will always proceed in this respect on the basis most economic for the department. But I am sure he will not quarrel with me if I do not go further at this time, because the whole system of asking for tenders in this field is not as simple as in other departments.
It certainly is not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Along the polar shelf, where you are dealing with vast distances, of course it is not as simple as it is in other departments.
You get the company with the biggest accident record.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend is speaking of other factors. I have heard this argued back and forth in the house, but I am not prepared to speak in relation to it one way or the other. I am only prepared to say that I am advised that, in fact, the most economic contract for the government of Canada was that which was entered into. If the letter of intent is succeeded by a contract for the coming year, it will be the most economic one for the government of Canada.
Now, I am advised that of the three proposals received, taken on an over-all basis, there is no question but that the lowest was that of the company to whom the letter of intent has been issued, but in respect of which company no contract has yet been entered into, and the formal terms are still under negotiation. The statement made by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, in fact, is totally accurate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I do
not believe I can sit here and listen to what the parliamentary secretary has said without making the kind of retort that the answer deserves, and that is that the statement made by the minister is wholly inaccurate. I will give you an example of why it is wholly inaccurate. When the minister's predecessor was in office I put on the order paper a series of questions, one of which had to do with this very matter. The question was whether or not a contract had been entered into in respect of helicopter service for the polar continental shelf. The reply was, no, but that a letter of intent had been given. This being the case in so far as the predecessor of the present Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys was concerned, why did we not get the same answer from the present minister? The answer which the minister has given is not only inaccurate but it is not in accordance with the facts. Once a letter of intent has been given that is, legally at least, tantamount to a contract. There have to be some very strong extenuating circumstances if a contract is not awarded, particularly if money is spent on behalf of the contractor arising out of the letter of intent. I presume the contractor is always in a position to say that, because in this case almost 27 days have elapsed since the letter of intent was given. Surely, the letter of intent has been acted upon and it is equivalent to a contract.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I feel satisfied that there will not be a slip on this occasion. I know that on two previous occasions, one involving an expenditure of $170,000 and the other $231,000, letters of intent went out in the same manner as in this case, if my memory serves me right, and again for the period March to August, 1962, there is a letter of intent involving the sum of $275,000. I have no doubt about it, having regard to what has taken place in the past; but I do have a great deal of doubt about the manner in which these contracts, in these three separate instances, have been awarded.
I am satisfied in my mind that they have not been awarded in accordance with the practice that prevails in other departments, and it is not an excuse to say that the circumstances in respect to the polar continental shelf are such that we have to adopt other methods. But one thing I will not let pass, sir, is these repeated and erroneous references of the parliamentary secretary to the practice in the past. We demonstrated last night, by reference to the very last day of supplementary estimates under the previous government, that most of the afternoon of that day was taken up, not by Mr. Harris answering questions through his parliamentary secretary while he was off in British Columbia, because Mr. Harris stayed in the house and attended to his job here, but what happened on that occasion was that because there were some very controversial questions about the Department of Citizenship and Immigration the then minister satisfied the committee by answering those questions at considerable length. We have not taken any exception in regard to the more or less non-controversial items, for which we do not expect the minister to be here, but when something of this magnitude comes up, when there is a question of whether the committee has been misled, surely it should not be left to the parliamentary secretary, however able he is, to have to defend ministers. It is the ministers, not parliamentary secretaries, who are responsible to this house, and a responsible minister would be here to defend his good name and his reputation, which is certainly under very serious question as a result of the answers given on March 21 and in the light of the fact that this letter of intent had been given on March 2 and to all practical intents and purposes this company had been told it was going to have this business.

His second proposal, and the one to which I take particular objection, had to do with the payment of possibly all but certainly the greater part of these expenses out of the public treasury.
To deal with the first question first, I do not think there is any disagreement among the parties or among the various members of the house that some means must be found to apply some reasonable limit. One can argue that there is a natural law or natural correcting process in force in that if a political party or an individual candidate in a constituency is clearly spending a great deal of money in an attempt to win an election the public becomes aware of the wide disparity between individual candidates or parties, and the good common sense of the Canadian people is very likely to counteract that. I offer in support of that view an incident which occurred in the electoral history of this country where a candidate spent a total of $75,000 and the reaction of the electorate in that constituency was precisely that which I have indicated. They were offended at the suggestion that someone with a great deal of money could come into that constituency and expect to be elected simply because he had more money than anyone else. I do not recall precisely, but if my memory serves me correctly the gentleman in question, having expended that amount of money, lost his deposit. That there should be some limit applied and some practical method followed to make that limit effective no one will deny.
I do suggest to the hon. member that there are prodigious difficulties in connection with any attempts that have been made to apply this limit. The difficulties I mentioned before in this house involve such things as the evaluation of various services which are rendered to individual candidates. I have in mind the value involved in a person who leaves his normal form of gainful employment to devote his entire energies to the support of a particular candidate. This is an expense in the true sense of the word. The man is foregoing the opportunity to earn money and is, in effect, making a contribution to the candidate of the amount of money he is not earning at that particular time.
Then, too, in my constituency certain of my friends and supporters make available their recreation rooms for committee rooms. While these items of expense never appear and will never appear on my election expense list, there are elements of value in placing a recreation room or an empty room in an office building at the disposal of a candidate

because these places could be rented to others. There is value involved. You can go through the various components that make up an election organization and you find these difficulties that I have mentioned before. I mention, too, the situation which arose in one constituency where labour organizers from all sections of the country were mobilized in that one constituency. Clearly, there was value involved. These men were not doing what they were being paid to do by the organization which normally pays their salaries. These are some of the difficulties that the hon. member is going to encounter in connection with this proposal.
Legislation has been enacted in various countries and jurisdictions in an attempt to accomplish this end. In fact, complete control or anything near complete control in this field has escaped those pursuing this goal. I am not suggesting for a moment that simply because there are prodigious difficulties we should not proceed, but it seems to me that we can reasonably expect little effective action in exploring this area. According to the statement made by the hon. gentleman which I read to the house a few minutes ago, he felt that all campaign expenses should be paid by the public treasury. In this connection, there was an article published recently in the Star Weekly written by a gentleman by the name of Rae Corelli in which this question was discussed in general terms. The article quotes an hon. member of this house, as follows: Skeena's Frank Howard opposes a treasury subsidy on the grounds that political parties would "tend to lose contact with the people".
Then, later, there appears a more interesting comment from a person described as a high level civil servant, and I quote:

Apparently all candidates would be given a certain amount of money, depending in part on the number of constituents involved and having regard also to certain other factors such as those encountered by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Henderson) and the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) and other areas where transportation difficulties are the overriding factor, rather than the number of voters. My solution, and the principle involved in this bill, have to do with a solution which will remove some of the possibilities giving rise to areas of abuse inherent in this whole question. The value to be placed on this bill-not the value to be placed on the explanatory note accompanying it-is evidenced by the amount of time which the hon. member spent dealing with it. Some 17 minutes of his time limit were spent in a negative approach to something else, and the balance of three minutes to advocating support for the bill now before us. He had no refuting remarks to make about the proposals which we have been putting forward for quite a number of years.
We should differentiate between what the explanatory note says the bill will do and what the bill itself will actually accomplish. The explanatory note says it is "as a convenience in making campaign contributions". The title refers to "campaign contributions" but the substance of the bill itself has nothing to do with this particular question. Were the bill to become law it would be nothing more than a smokescreen to cover up for the pork barrel artists who assist the two old line parties now represented by the government and the principal party in opposition.
There was an article in Maclean's magazine a few months ago in which a former Liberal organizer, campaigner, or something of that nature, made comments about things which existed within the party so far as campaign contributions were concerned. He wrote that it is the general practice for large corporations to divide their campaign contributions on the basis of 60 per cent to the party in

Canada Elections Act
office and 40 per cent to the party in opposition. The article referred to by my hon. friend from York-Scarborough, which was written by Rae Corelli in the Star Weekly, gives a similar indication. I do not know where Mr. Corelli got his information. I do not know if his article is as authoritative as that I referred to earlier, but nevertheless he gave the same indication with regard to campaign contributions by private corporations.
Obviously they operate on the principle that if you have two horses in a race and bribe both the jockeys, then your chance of winning is pretty good. This bill deals only with candidates, and only requires a candidate to file his source of income and method of expenditure. It does not require the same information to be provided by political parties, and our major concern should be for the interest and welfare of the general public.
In my judgment this bill will not take one step towards protecting the public against encroachments that may be made upon their property and rights of freedom by political parties. It does nothing to make sure that secret contributions will come under public scrutiny. It does nothing to deal with the question of whether there should be a limit placed upon the amount of money that can be spent by a candidate and a party. It does nothing whatsoever to deal with the possibility, remote or otherwise of a recurrence of something akin to the Beauharnois scandal that existed not too many years ago, and it does nothing to prevent a recurrence of the awkward situation in which Sir John A. Macdonald found himself with respect to party contributions. It does nothing whatsover to prevent a recurrence of something similar to the Somers scandal which existed in the structure of the provincial government of British Columbia not too long ago. All it will do is place more work upon the shoulders of the returning officers because they are required by one of the provisions of the bill to give to the various postmasters a list containing the names, addresses and occupations of the candidates and the official agents.
It will overload the postal employees, who are overloaded in any event at election time. Its sole purpose is to disseminate by householder mailing system the name, address and occupation of the candidate and the official agent. I submit that if one wants to accomplish this sort of thing and if, as the hon. member for York-Scarborough says, there are a number of people who would like to contribute to the party of their choice but who have not done so because they have not been asked, this is valuable information for the parties themselves and for the candidate, and I think it would be a worth-while expenditure for the

candidate, his official agent or his campaign committee to invest some money in a householder mailing system and in effect say, "This is our candidate. This is what we believe in. If you would like to contribute, this is the address to which you can send your contribution". This would be a far better way of approaching the question of asking for campaign fund contributions from the individual citizens of this nation than by overloading the returning officer and the public treasury by having to pay for the householder mailing system.
I have other thoughts about this matter which apply to candidates themselves, but these are not connected with the question of campaign fund contributions. We have made suggestions and proposed ideas in years past on this question, and will continue to do so. I think it is an excellent system which exists at the moment, where all three parties are represented in the House of Commons, each expressing ideas and making suggestions and proposals as to how we can deal with the question of campaign fund contributions and how we can ensure that parties remain in close liaison or rapport with the general public.
I doubt very much that we will come to any agreement on what approach should be made before that time arises to which the Prime Minister made reference today, but I hope we will be able to keep alive in the minds of the parties themselves, no matter which one is in government or which parties are represented in the house, after the election this idea that we should be tackling this problem in more than a casual way. I hope these proposals which are being made are not merely election gimmicks to present a picture of purity to the general public before the election takes place.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DISTRIBUTION OF NAMES OF CANDIDATES
speechtext:
The last two speakers have, in effect, found nothing wrong with the principles contained in this bill but they have made certain suggestions which indicate that they look askance at the methods employed. It is elementary that if there is a good principle we can always modify the legislation to suit the circumstances. When one looks at the bill together with the explanatory notes it seems to me to
IMr. Deschatelets.l
be based on excellent principles and if the house were to decide to pass the measure it would be simple enough to add a section or a subsection saying it is the intention that those voters who desire to participate by making a contribution to a party or candidate were receiving a sheet, or information, for that purpose.
If it were decided that it would be good for a form to be used, it would be elementary to put at the bottom of the form a statement that those desiring to make a contribution to support a party or candidate whose names were shown might do so. This would achieve the result which the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) wishes to achieve.
A bill of this kind is probably a considerable improvement over the existing practice and I think we should support it because it is substantially better than an alternative which has been offered and which has been the subject of some discussion in an earlier debate, namely that all this should be done through what is, in effect, a government expenditure. I submit that government is too much with us now.
There is a tendency on the part of many voters to consider themselves as having little or no part in government. They think of themselves and of the government as being completely distinct. If a democratic system is to flourish and improve it can only be with the participation of those who comprise the electorate. I submit that the effect of putting into the hands of the government all the campaign expenses would remove from the people a considerable incentive to participate. It would add to the distance which all too often separates the voter from the government. We saw too much of this in years past. Until 1957, as a result of the war and conditions following it, there was a system developing of government by revelation, government by a few favoured individuals who thought they had this divine right. In 1957 and 1958, the people of this country ended that phase and restored control to members of parliament. They will confirm and endorse that decision at a certain date which I hope is not too far removed. To that extent, the greater participation which will inevitably result from the adoption of the bill would be all to the good. I think of a statement made by a very eminent young man, who now holds an important position in the free world, when he was faced with accepting great responsibility. That statement may very well be applied to the principle of the bill we are now considering. He said: Think not of what your country can do for you, but of what you can do for your country.

I think this is the spirit in which people should approach the question of government and the election of members of parliament. Not everyone has the time or opportunity to participate in the administration of the country. All cannot be members of parliament or returning officers. However, if people had the opportunity of making these contributions and felt it was the thing to do they would have a sense of participation and would have a definite interest in election campaigns and their results.
In my limited experience I have found that when we return to our constituencies we encounter a great reservoir of common sense, good judgment and sound understanding. Certainly this was demonstrated in March of 1958 as I am sure it will be again.
I know that others wish to participate in this debate and although there is more I should like to say I will conclude my remarks. To the extent to which I am certain this measure will tend to result in more people becoming interested in political campaigns I am glad to endorse the principle behind the bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DISTRIBUTION OF NAMES OF CANDIDATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I commence by paying a massive tribute to the sponsor of this bill, the hon. member for York-Scarborough. When he made reference to history's most impartial chairman in the debate between the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the future defeated N.D.P. candidate in Regina city, I think the hon. member for York-Scarborough with that reference paid one of history's greatest compliments to a father-in-law. The Ottawa Journal please copy.
I do not share the feeling of my colleagues in the Conservative party who have previously spoken in this debate. I would have a natural reluctance, I am afraid, if the taxpayers of this country should be asked to pay the costs of sending the names of candidates and official agents around from door to door, even though I realize, as the bill sets out, all the candidates in a particular riding would be lumped together.
I look upon this matter very much as I think I would if I were a bachelor to whom someone sent a list of all the eligible young spinsters in the neighbourhood whom I might court. I think politics should be approached very much on the same basis as romance in that one should seek out, look around, hunt and woo as best one possibly can and the road should never be made too easy.
Further, I suggest I do not think the public would give general acceptance to a bill in which they would be asked to pay part of the expense of a political campaign. No matter how highly we regard ourselves in this honourable chamber, outside I think people
Business of the House
would entertain a certain suspicion-and probably a well justified suspicion-if we should adopt the measure that is proposed by the hon. member.
May I point out a fallacy in the sponsor's argument. This concerns the reference to the Gallup poll in the United States in which apparently some 17 million people-I presume this would be a projection from their interviews with a few hundred thousand people or families-would favour giving $5 apiece to their favourite political party if only machinery could be set up to collect that money. Presumably those 17 million at one time or another in the last United States campaign heard of Mr. Nixon or Mr. Kennedy, and presumably there were enough advertisements everywhere to show where these donations might have gone. I would therefore ask the hon. member why at least part of the 17 million, a substantial number-say over half-did not make those $5 donations. I think the measure he proposed for this country would have very much the same result.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock.
